title: Ten avatars, one Vishnu
word: the ten avatars as a series
hookLine: a row of pictures, one refrain, and every shape is Vishnu
carry: avatara: one vishnu, coming down every age
tomorrow: a fish the size of a fingertip asks a king for help. why?

lines: A PROFILE PICTURE, OR A DESCENT?
cards: Avatar, these days, is a profile picture or a character in a game. It's Sanskrit first.

On some calendar prints and temple walls there's a row of pictures: a fish, a tortoise, a boar, a figure with a lion's head, a small boy with an umbrella, and on down the row. Every one of them is Vishnu.
And there's an old song that walks along that row, with a refrain that keeps coming back after every verse: jaya jagadisha hare. Today is about that sound, and the row it holds together.

teach.b: Avatara means a descent, a coming down. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says, in paraphrase, that whenever dharma fails and wrong rises, he comes, age after age, to protect the good and set things right.

teach.h: ONE LIST OF TEN, AND OTHERS.
teach.b: The Puranas tell those comings as stories, and one list of ten became a series: Matsya the fish, Kurma the tortoise, Varaha the boar, Narasimha the man-lion, Vamana the dwarf, Parashurama, Rama, Krishna, the Buddha in some lists and Balarama in others, and Kalki, still to come.
The lists don't all agree; the Bhagavata Purana names more than ten. Now the sound. In the Gita Govinda, the poet Jayadeva sings a hymn to the ten.
Each verse names one descent and ends the same way: jaya jagadisha hare, victory, Hari, lord of the world.

teach.h: THE SHAPES CHANGE. THE REFRAIN DOESN'T.
teach.b: The shapes change, verse after verse. The refrain doesn't.
That's the series in one sound: a fish in the flood, a boar under the earth, a prince with a bow, the same one coming down in whatever shape that age's trouble calls for.
Some readers see a pattern in the order, from water to land to the human world; others take each descent on its own. Either way, the row starts in the water, with a fish.

how: Images of Vishnu's ten avatars appear in a row on some temple walls and household prints, and Jayadeva's hymn to the ten, from the Gita Govinda, is sung in devotional settings, with its refrain repeated after every verse.

games.q: what does “the ten avatars as a series” mean?
o: a set of game characters from old Indian art
Vishnu's descents, read as one row of shapes
ten separate gods who guard the world in turn

games.q: the start of the row — tap the pairs.
p: the fish, first in the row

games.q: your little cousin points at the fish and the tortoise on Nani's calendar and asks if they're 'different gods.' what's the row's answer?
o: one Vishnu, coming down in a different shape each time.
different gods, each one stronger than the last.
different gods who take turns guarding the world.
games.why: the row is one Vishnu in many shapes, whatever each age's trouble calls for. the refrain says it: the verse changes, the one praised doesn't.

practice: Pick one sound that keeps coming back where you are: a clock, a fan, traffic outside, your own breath. Each time it returns, notice it's the same sound in a new moment, like a refrain after a new verse.
If you pray, you can let the refrain run quietly under your breath: jaya jagadisha hare.
